summary: Given a sorted array and a target, return the 1-based indices of the two numbers that sum to the target using O(1) extra space.
mainInsight: Because the array is sorted, the sum of the two ends is monotone: if it is too big the right end can never be part of an answer, if too small the left end can never be. Move the offending pointer and discard that element for good.

approaches.name: Hash map
approaches.summary: Same as Two Sum with a dict.
weaknesses: Ignores sortedness and uses extra space

approaches.name: Binary search for the complement
approaches.summary: For each i binary-search target - numbers[i].

approaches.name: Two pointers from both ends
approaches.summary: l=0, r=n-1; move l up if the sum is too small, r down if too large.

promptVariants: Which technique exploits the sorted order in Two Sum II?
What pattern gives O(n) time and O(1) space on a sorted array pair-sum?
cards.explanation: Sorted order makes the pair sum monotone in each pointer.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Hash map of complements: Works, but O(n) space - the problem asks for O(1).

promptVariants: Why is it safe to discard numbers[r] when numbers[l] + numbers[r] > target?
State why moving a pointer never skips the answer.
cards.answer: numbers[r] is paired with the smallest still-possible partner numbers[l]; if even that sum is too big, every other partner (all >= numbers[l]) is also too big. So numbers[r] cannot be in any answer and can be dropped. The symmetric argument holds for l.
cards.explanation: This is the correctness proof of every converging two-pointer search.

promptVariants: Time complexity of the two-pointer solution: ___
Two Sum II runs in ___ time.
cards.explanation: Each iteration moves one pointer inward; at most n-1 moves.

promptVariants: Extra space of the two-pointer solution: ___
Two Sum II needs ___ auxiliary space.
Your loop uses `while l <= r`. Is that or `l < r` more precise, and why does the answer still come out right?
What does `l == r` mean in the two-pointer search?
cards.answer: `l < r` is the precise condition: l == r would use one element twice. Since the problem guarantees exactly one valid pair of distinct indices, the l == r state is never reached with total == target for the true answer, so it is harmless but looser than needed.
cards.explanation: Use the tight condition in interviews.
